synopsis: The plan must satisfy skeptical executive, finance and product-liability readers by closing weaknesses rather than adding upside; research on 3,667 Marie Curie applications supports that approach, while 43 reviewers assessing the same 25 NIH applications showed essentially no agreement, cautioning against assuming reviewer consensus [f9404, f207, f9845, f9846]. Executive-facing material should state the decision, deliverables and exclusions, deadline confidence, risks, fallback and resources, with auditable deadline probabilities rather than merely a planned date [f9854, f16337, f16443]. Finance wants cheap early experiments and bottom-up post-pilot estimates before larger commitments: savings may be counted before physical-test substitution is earned, reuse across machine families remains unproven, and independent off-road return-on-investment evidence and recurring-cost information were not found [f16553, f16442, f16560, f16562, f16561, f16563]. Reviewers should approve specific virtual substitutions within validated envelopes, supported by a one-page credibility map, and see a representative safety/legal evidence package months before launch to reduce the critical risk of late rejection [f16557, f16556, f14996, f11036]. Legal involvement at the end is too late: the liability reviewer needs jurisdiction-specific compliance analysis, authorizations, defensible substitutions, auditable provenance and retention, enforced operating limits, and reviewed claims and warnings [f10848, f16565, f16566]. Legal sign-off must address Product Liability Directive disclosure, its application to products placed on the market after 9 December 2026 and treatment of software as a product, Machinery Regulation conformity from 20 January 2027, and the AI Act if applicable [f10849, f16568, f16569, f10850, f10851].
